profiles.meeting_scenario: Two colleagues are holding a brainstorming meeting about how to turn the first offering of a new Creative Problem Solving course into a conference proposal and possible internal study. The course combined in-class creativity games, formal problem-solving methodologies such as design thinking, SCAMPER, and TRIZ, team product-development assignments, and multiple leadership rotations with self- and peer-assessment. The agenda is to generate promising ways to describe the course, identify what evidence they already have, and sketch a compelling angle for comparing methodologies and showing changes in students' views of creativity and leadership. The expected outcome is a short list of candidate study/storyline ideas and an informal division of follow-up tasks.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Creativity pedagogy, project-based learning, facilitation of team innovation exercises
members.background: Lena designed and taught the new course after several years running interdisciplinary innovation workshops for engineering, business, and arts students.
members.private_state: She wants the course to be seen as distinctive because of its hands-on classroom energy and leadership practice, and she is especially eager to preserve evidence from the smaller in-class activities that she feels outsiders often undervalue.
hidden_assumptions: A 'leadership opportunity' includes short in-class facilitation turns during games and problem-solving sprints, not only the larger graded project-lead roles.
Students' perceptions of creativity are visible in reflective writing, debrief comments, and the language they use about creativity, even without a tightly repeated survey instrument.
When people mention 'peer leadership assessments,' they are usually referring to the quick feedback forms teammates completed right after each leadership rotation.
Students from the honors innovation lab who joined the team projects are part of the practical course cohort because they did the same activities and influenced team dynamics.

members.name: Marcus Chen
members.expertise: Program evaluation, classroom assessment design, educational analytics for curricular pilots
members.background: Marcus supports faculty in converting teaching innovations into credible assessment narratives for accreditation reports, grants, and scholarship-of-teaching presentations.
members.private_state: He wants to shape the brainstorm into a study that can be summarized cleanly and defended methodologically, ideally using data structures that are already institutional and easy to analyze.
hidden_assumptions: A 'leadership opportunity' means one of the formally assigned team-lead roles attached to the major problem-solving or product-development projects.
Claims about students' perceptions are strongest when backed by repeated, comparable measures such as pre/post items or common end-of-module rating scales.
The phrase 'team-member assessments' or 'peer assessments' normally refers to the end-of-semester LMS peer-evaluation packet because that is the standard analyzable record.
The 'pilot cohort' or 'course data' means students officially enrolled in the course sections and covered by the standard course-evaluation workflow.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a leadership opportunity
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about students having 'two leadership opportunities' and comparing first versus second leadership experiences.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means any two occasions when a student led peers, including brief in-class facilitation during creativity games, sprints, or mini-challenges.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the two formally designated lead roles attached to the larger graded team assignments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The course materials really did promise multiple leadership opportunities, so the phrase sounds settled and familiar; neither expects that the other is counting different kinds of leadership episodes under the same wording.

misalignment_points.topic: Which peer assessment data they mean
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'peer assessments' or 'team-member assessments' as if there is one obvious dataset.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking about the short Google Forms completed immediately after each leadership rotation, often tied to a specific class activity or project checkpoint.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking about the end-of-semester LMS peer-evaluation survey that summarizes teamwork and leadership more globally.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both instruments involve teammates rating one another's leadership, and both were genuinely used in the course, so the shorthand label sounds specific enough even though each person is picturing a different record.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as evidence of student perceptions
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they want to show 'student perceptions of creativity' and how those perceptions shifted across methodologies.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this can be shown through reflection prompts, exit tickets, debrief notes, and examples of how students describe creativity after activities.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this really requires repeated, comparable perception measures, such as the same survey items administered pre/post or at multiple points.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In education conversations, 'perceptions' is a broad and cooperative-sounding term that comfortably covers both qualitative and quantitative evidence, so each person hears confirmation of their own evidentiary standard.

misalignment_points.topic: Who belongs in the pilot cohort
misalignment_points.surface_form: They talk about analyzing 'the pilot cohort' or 'course data' without narrowing who is included.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes the officially enrolled students plus five honors innovation lab students who joined the product-development teams and completed many of the same activities.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes only the students rostered in the official course sections, since those are the students he assumes belong in the clean course dataset.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The extra students were visibly embedded in teams and classroom activities, so from an instructional perspective they feel like part of the course; from an assessment perspective, rostered enrollment is the silent default, and neither side feels a need to specify it during an early brainstorm.

turns.inner_thought: I want the proposal to foreground what made this course alive: the hands-on sequences, the quick facilitation turns, and the way students' language about creativity opened up over time. When I say two leadership opportunities, I'm thinking of those two moments when each student stepped up to guide peers during the in-class activities, because those are where I saw real growth. And for student perceptions of creativity, we already have plenty in the reflections, debriefs, and exit comments even if it wasn't all on one repeated instrument.
turns.utterance: What I’d really love is a conference angle that captures how the course changed students’ perceptions of creativity across the different methodologies, and also how that connects to the two leadership opportunities built into the class.

turns.inner_thought: That could be a strong assessment story if we anchor it in analyzable records. If we can connect changes in student perceptions of creativity to peer assessments across the pilot cohort, that starts to sound methodologically defensible and easy to summarize. I’m assuming the pilot cohort means the enrolled students in the official sections, and peer assessments means the standard LMS set at the end of the term.
turns.utterance: Yes, that feels promising. We might frame it around changes in student perceptions of creativity and tie that to the peer assessments across the pilot cohort.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he sees the value. I should keep the methodologies visible and make sure we don't flatten everything into the big projects. The debrief comments right after the design thinking sprint, the SCAMPER sequence, and the TRIZ challenge really show how students were rethinking creativity, and because those were attached to each leadership turn, we can compare how they sounded across the two leadership opportunities.
turns.utterance: One way in would be to compare student reactions after the design thinking sprint, the SCAMPER sequence, and the TRIZ-based challenge, and use the debrief comments from each leadership turn to show how those perceptions moved.

turns.inner_thought: A comparison table would work nicely if we keep the variables clean. We can line up methodology, first versus second leadership opportunity, and the peer assessments. In my head, that means the two formal lead assignments and the end-of-semester peer-evaluation packet, which should give us a tidy structure.
turns.utterance: I can already see a simple comparison table: methodology on one axis, then first-versus-second leadership opportunity patterns, and the peer assessments alongside that.

turns.inner_thought: And the dataset is actually richer than just the roster, because those honors innovation lab students were fully embedded in the teams and did the same reflections and activities. They absolutely matter for the classroom story, especially around how students talked about creativity in the moment. I should flag that now so he builds the study around the full experience.
turns.utterance: Also, the dataset should be richer than it might sound at first, because the honors innovation lab students were embedded in the project teams and completed the same reflection prompts, so the pilot cohort gives us a lot to work with.

turns.inner_thought: Interesting. If the pilot cohort is larger, that may help the story, though I’ll need to see what counts as part of the official records. The main practical question is whether the team-member assessments are complete in the LMS for everyone I’m expecting to include, because that’s the analyzable source I know how to pull quickly.
turns.utterance: That definitely makes the pilot cohort more interesting. Do you know whether the team-member assessments are complete for everyone in the LMS records?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the quick forms were done after each facilitation round, so we should have a strong set. Those immediate peer responses are exactly what I want preserved, because they catch the small leadership moments people usually ignore. And when I think about students sounding more confident about creativity by the second leadership opportunity, that’s visible in those comments and ratings tied right to the activity.
turns.utterance: Yes, we should be in good shape there. We had quick post-activity forms after each facilitation round, and those should help us see whether students sounded more confident about creativity by the second leadership opportunity.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then the records are probably there in some form. I’m picturing grouping the course data by methodology and looking at whether peer ratings improve from the first to the second lead assignment for the enrolled students. That gives us a clean, reportable arc without overcomplicating things.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Then we could group results by methodology and check whether peer ratings improve from the first to the second leadership opportunity across the course data.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep steering this toward the playful classroom work, not let everything collapse into the major project frame. The games and short exercises were where students most visibly shifted how they described creativity and how they enacted leadership with one another. That distinctive energy is the course’s real contribution.
turns.utterance: And I’d want the story to emphasize that even the more playful in-class activities shifted how students talked about creativity and leadership, not only the major projects.

turns.inner_thought: That gives us a workable division of labor. I’ll draft an analysis plan for the pilot cohort using the peer assessments and whatever comparable perception measures we have access to, and she can gather artifacts that help illustrate the narrative. If the data structures line up, this could become both a conference proposal and a credible internal study.
turns.utterance: That sounds like a good split, then. I’ll sketch an analysis plan for the pilot cohort using the peer assessments and the perception measures, and you can pull representative student artifacts that help us tell the story.
